Let's begin with a very simple introduction to Information Theory: what it is, why it was created (important), what problems it solves etc. However, before we get deep into Shannon's work, I'd like to structure this inquiry as if it were an introductory study into this field.

Apart from the complex mathematics, the "story" of information theory (based on what I currently know...) is something like...

Alpha

"Beginning with the name, 'Information Theory' we can essentially inquire it as Theoretical in understanding. It's applications therefore span various THeoretical fields of Application and Implementation Science, from Computation to Communication Systems in diverse forms (unsure of examples for the latter...)."

Concretion 1

"However Information-Theory is interested in a fine selection of these appliactions; specifically information, structure and entropy as the base objects of study; the central orbit of the field."

Concretion 2

"...The purpose of the study of information and it's theoretical structures and applications, is in understanding how information (and it's lifecycles in systems) behaves when subject to diverse conditions. Such conditions are present in all Systems of Communcation, and Information in some sense, is the exchange of Communication (unsure of this, becuase it's closer to Cybernetic Theory). A core problem in Information Theory is signal degradation; all problems eventually trace back to the base problem; Entropy (information loss/uncertainty/noise, etc.)"

Quantifying Information (Value Theory(?))

"Information is measured decoupled from meaning, as linguistics deals with the semantics pragmatics of content, Information-Theory is interested in probing the inner workings of information; at the level of structure. This however, is prone to Entropy itself; Information is fundmanetally incomplete without a System, and it's observed conditions in the Real-world."

I am unsure if that is an accurate introduction, or if it captures the heart of the problem...

It is quite fascinating to think that one can study "bits" of information and eventually develop a Computer, capable of the web, music and technologies not originally planned (Synergy & Emergence.)

This is actually what Lambda Calculus maximizes; and it inspired most programming languages today. I think Lamda Calculus is Orthogonal or in a nearby neighboorhood of related subject matter... forming a network of understanding in this case, is incredibly on topic!

"1" Can mean essentially anything (and in CS, it is often the case that a given bit can be assigned virtually any meaning, so long as it remains stable (which is the structural aspect of meaning and information binding... Language needs this otherwise words, sounds and meaning are convoluted and Communication is degraded or impossible... interestingly enough, this traces back to the original purpose of Information Theory))
